title: The Spark of Life

image.credit: collection not stated on source page; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: A collage-style drawing of an airship, a flying machine, with cut-out pieces, bright colors and small notes, in the manner of an outsider artist's notebook page.

source.museum: collection not stated on source page
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, years, medium, public-domain statement); collection not stated on the page

context: A collage by Charles Dellschau, dated 1899 to 1900 on its source page, which tags it Airships and Outsider Art. Dellschau, a German-born American, is widely known for fanciful airship pictures; the page does not state the collection.

descriptions.k: This is a flying machine, like a big airship. It is made with cut paper and drawings. Which parts do you see? Where would you fly?
descriptions.g12: Charles Dellschau made this picture with cut pieces and drawings. It shows a flying airship with lots of small parts. Look at the colors and details. If you could fly it, where would you go?
descriptions.g35: Charles Dellschau made The Spark of Life as a collage in 1899 to 1900. The page tags it Airships and Outsider Art, meaning the artist worked outside the usual art schools. A collage is made by gluing pieces together. How do the cut-out parts and details make an airship feel real or imagined?
descriptions.g68: The Spark of Life (1899-1900) is a collage by Charles Dellschau, tagged on its page as Airships and Outsider Art. Outsider Art describes makers who work outside formal art training. The picture combines drawn and assembled pieces to imagine a flying machine. How do collage and detail turn an imagined machine into something that seems plausible?
descriptions.g910: Charles Dellschau's The Spark of Life (1899-1900) is a collage tagged Airships and Outsider Art. As an outsider artist, Dellschau developed his own visual world rather than following academic rules. How does the layering of drawn and cut elements build a private technical vision, and how does the label Outsider Art shape what we expect from the work?
descriptions.g1112: The Spark of Life (1899-1900) belongs to the body of airship imagery associated with Charles Dellschau, whom the page tags as an Outsider Art maker. Such work invites questions about invention, fantasy and who gets labeled an artist. How might the collage be read as technical drawing, imaginative art or personal archive, and what do the page's limited facts allow us to claim?

teacherNote.context: A collage from 1899 to 1900 by Charles Dellschau, tagged Airships and Outsider Art on its source page, which does not state the collection. Outsider Art refers to makers working outside formal art training.
directions: Have students design their own flying machine using cut paper pieces, then explain what each part does.
Ask students to compare a collage with a drawing of the same subject and discuss what each can do.
Discuss what makes someone an artist and why labels like Outsider Art are used.
